deck.title: Snow Family
deck.analogy: Never underestimate the bandwidth of a truck full of hard drives: AWS ships you a rugged encrypted box, you fill it locally, and ship it back to be loaded into S3.

cards.front: Why does the Snow Family exist?

back.answer: Network bandwidth is a physical limit; Snow devices ship data physically instead of uploading it.
back.explanation: 100 TB over 100 Mbps takes roughly 100+ days. You copy data locally at LAN speed, ship the device back, and AWS loads it into S3.
back.mnemonic: A truck full of hard drives has huge bandwidth.

cards.front: Snow Family: what is the rule of thumb for choosing a Snow device over network transfer?

back.answer: If network transfer would take more than about a week, use a Snow device.

cards.front: What compute capability do Snow devices offer, and why does it matter?

back.answer: They run EC2 instances and Lambda functions on-board, enabling edge computing without internet.
back.explanation: Useful on ships at sea, in mines, at military bases and at remote research stations.

cards.front: Snow Family: what are the capacity and use case of Snowcone?

back.answer: 8–14 TB; tiny, rugged, ships anywhere (even by drone); for small edge sites.

cards.front: Snow Family: what are the capacity and use case of Snowball Edge Storage Optimized?

back.answer: About 80 TB usable; the workhorse for ~50–500 TB migrations (order several).

cards.front: Snow Family: what distinguishes Snowball Edge Compute Optimized?

back.answer: Less storage, more CPU plus optional GPU; for edge processing with EC2/Lambda where there's no connectivity.

cards.front: Snow Family: what is Snowmobile's capacity and when should you consider it?

back.answer: Up to 100 PB; a shipping-container truck, considered at more than 10 PB.

cards.front: Which Snow device comes with the DataSync agent preinstalled?

back.answer: Snowcone.
back.explanation: Copy data onto it, then sync back online later or ship the device.

cards.front: How do you handle a 200 TB migration with Snow devices?

back.answer: Order several Snowball Edge Storage Optimized devices in parallel (about 3 × 80 TB).

cards.front: What is AWS OpsHub?

back.answer: The GUI application for managing Snow devices, no CLI needed.

cards.front: What are the steps of the Snow Family process?

back.answer: Order in console, AWS ships, copy data locally (KMS-encrypted), ship back, AWS loads into S3 and wipes device.
back.explanation: The E Ink shipping label updates itself.

cards.front: How is data encrypted when copied onto a Snow device?

back.answer: Automatically with KMS; keys never live on the device in usable form.

cards.front: Can Snowball import data directly into S3 Glacier?

back.answer: No. Data always lands in S3 first; use an S3 lifecycle rule to transition to Glacier.
back.explanation: Any answer choice saying import from Snowball straight to Glacier is wrong.

cards.front: Which Snow device suits a vessel collecting sensor data with intermittent connectivity, and how?

back.answer: Snowball Edge Compute Optimized: run EC2 AMIs and Lambda locally, then ship or sync results later.

cards.front: Migrate 200 TB; the site has a 100 Mbps link and a 3-week deadline. Which solution?

back.answer: Snowball Edge Storage Optimized (a few 80 TB units).
back.explanation: Network math means months, so ship devices.

cards.front: Decommissioning a datacenter: multiple petabytes (>10 PB) to AWS. Which service?

back.answer: Snowmobile.

choices.why: Too many devices at this scale.

cards.front: A research ship must run analysis on collected data with no internet connectivity. Which device?

back.answer: Snowball Edge Compute Optimized (GPU if ML is mentioned).
back.explanation: Compute happens at the disconnected edge.

choices.why: A management GUI, not a device.

cards.front: A company wants to archive 80 TB directly into S3 Glacier using Snowball. What is the answer?

back.answer: Import to S3, then use a lifecycle rule to transition to Glacier.
back.explanation: Snowball can't write to Glacier directly.

choices.text: Import to S3, then lifecycle rule to Glacier

cards.front: A small remote clinic must transfer ~8–10 TB from a space- and power-constrained site. Which device?

back.answer: Snowcone.

cards.front: Transfer 40 TB once; it would take 6 weeks over the existing connection. Which approach?

back.answer: Snowball Edge.
back.explanation: More than 1 week over the wire means the Snow family.

choices.text: Wait six weeks over the network

choices.why: Over a week by network → Snow.

cards.front: How do you manage Snow devices with a graphical interface?

back.answer: AWS OpsHub.
